name: Guillotine Choke from Butterfly Guard
description: Master the Guillotine Choke from Butterfly Guard. Learn hook elevation setups, grip mechanics, and finishing details for this high-percentage blood choke.
summary: The Guillotine Choke from Butterfly Guard is a front-headlock blood choke launched from seated bottom, where active butterfly hooks drive the opponent's head down and elevate their hips to stretch the torso while the choking arm compresses both carotid arteries.
overview:
The Guillotine Choke from Butterfly Guard is one of the highest-percentage submission entries in modern grappling. The butterfly guard provides a unique platform for the guillotine because the hooks create immediate elevation threat, forcing the opponent to choose between defending the sweep and defending the choke. When an opponent drives forward to neutralize butterfly hooks or shoots for a takedown, they create the exact head-down posture that exposes the neck for guillotine entries. This natural offensive pairing makes the butterfly-guillotine combination a foundational attack chain.

What distinguishes this variant from standing or closed guard guillotines is the role of the butterfly hooks in both setup and finish. During the setup phase, the hooks provide constant upward pressure that prevents the opponent from posturing out or driving through. During the finishing phase, the bottom player uses hook elevation combined with a hip-back motion to stretch the opponent's body while tightening the choke, creating a powerful two-directional force that makes defense extremely difficult. The seated posture also allows for rapid grip acquisition and adjustment that flat-on-back positions cannot match.

Strategically, the butterfly guillotine serves as a critical deterrent against aggressive passing. Opponents who lean forward into butterfly guard or attempt to flatten the guard player expose themselves to snap-down entries and front headlock transitions that lead directly to the choke. This creates a dilemma where the passer must respect the guillotine threat, which in turn opens up sweeping opportunities. Elite grapplers use this dynamic interplay between sweep and submission to control the pace of engagement from butterfly guard bottom.

injury_risks.recovery_time: Immediate recovery but requires medical monitoring

safety_considerations.application_speed: SLOW and progressive - 3-5 seconds minimum application time. Never snap or jerk the submission
tap_signals: Verbal tap or any vocal sound
Physical hand tap on opponent or mat
Any distress signal or loss of resistance
release_protocol: Remove arm from around opponent's neck
Help opponent to seated position if unconscious
Call for medical assistance if partner does not immediately recover
training_restrictions: Never use competition speed in training
Always allow clear tap access for both arms
Stop immediately at any sign of distress
Avoid cranking or using neck hyperextension as a finishing mechanic
Never practice on training partners with existing neck injuries

variations_and_setups.description: Trap the opponent's arm inside the choke alongside their neck. The trapped arm blocks their ability to hand-fight or frame, and the extra limb compressed against the neck increases choking pressure on the far-side carotid artery.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: When the opponent reaches across your body or posts a hand on the mat during a pass attempt, trapping the arm naturally

variations_and_setups.description: After securing the chin strap grip, rotate the choking elbow high above the opponent's spine while pulling the wrist deep across the throat. This creates a tighter channel around the neck and targets both carotid arteries more precisely than a standard squeeze.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: When you have a deep grip and the opponent is defending by tucking the chin, as the high elbow angle bypasses chin defense

variations_and_setups.description: Use an aggressive two-on-one or collar tie snap-down to force the opponent's head below your shoulder line, then immediately thread the choking arm under the chin. The snap-down momentum makes the opponent's posture recovery much slower than their descent.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: Against opponents with strong upright posture who are not leaning forward enough to naturally expose the neck

attacker.name: from Butterfly Guard Attacker
attacker.description: Learn to attack the Guillotine Choke from Butterfly Guard with step-by-step finishing mechanics, grip configurations, and responses to common defenses.
attacker.overview: Attacking the Guillotine Choke from Butterfly Guard combines the sweeping threat of the hooks with the choking mechanics of the front headlock. The attacker uses the seated butterfly position to snap the opponent's head down, secure a chin strap or high-elbow grip around the neck, and finish by falling back with hook elevation to stretch the opponent while compressing the carotid arteries. The key advantage is that every sweep defense your opponent makes exposes the neck, and every guillotine defense they attempt weakens their base against sweeps. This creates a powerful offensive loop where neither threat can be ignored, forcing the opponent into increasingly compromised positions.
key_principles: Use butterfly hook pressure to force the opponent's weight forward and create head-down entries for the guillotine
Secure the choking grip fully before committing to the fall-back finish to avoid losing position on a failed attempt
Coordinate hook elevation with hip withdrawal to create opposing forces that stretch the spine and tighten the choke
Maintain control of the far arm or shoulder to prevent the opponent from circling to the safe side and escaping
Keep elbows pinched tight and squeeze the grip toward your sternum rather than pulling outward away from the body
Time the guillotine entry with the opponent's forward pressure or failed pass attempt for maximum head exposure
setup_requirements: Seated upright butterfly guard with both hooks active under opponent's thighs providing constant elevator pressure
Opponent's head driven below your shoulder level through snap-down, failed takedown, or forward weight commitment
Choking arm threaded under the opponent's chin with the wrist blade positioned against the near-side carotid artery
Non-choking hand secures a reinforcing grip (Gable grip, S-grip, or palm-to-palm) over the choking wrist
Far-side control through overhook, elbow clamp, or wrist grip to prevent opponent from circling to safety

execution_steps.action: Snap down and secure the head
execution_steps.description: From seated butterfly guard with active hooks, use a collar tie or two-on-one grip to snap your opponent's head below your shoulder line. Time this with their forward pressure or a failed pass attempt to minimize resistance. Your hooks maintain upward pressure throughout to prevent them from backing away or recovering posture.

Slide your choking arm under the opponent's chin, threading the wrist blade against the near-side carotid artery. Your forearm should cross the throat at an angle with the radius bone creating the primary choking surface. Keep the arm tight against your chest to prevent any space for the opponent to tuck their chin or insert a defensive hand.

Secure your hands together over the choking wrist using a Gable grip, S-grip, or palm-to-palm configuration. The non-choking hand reinforces the choking arm and prevents grip slippage under pressure. Pull both elbows tight to your ribcage to eliminate slack in the hold and maximize compression around the neck.

Clamp your non-choking elbow against the opponent's far shoulder or trap their far arm with an overhook. This prevents them from circling toward the choke side to create slack, posturing away to strip the grip, or establishing defensive frames against your chest. This control must be established before committing to the fall-back.

Begin falling backward while simultaneously driving your butterfly hooks upward into the opponent's inner thighs. This creates two opposing forces: your body weight pulls their head and neck downward and toward you while your hooks elevate their hips upward and away, stretching the spine and tightening the choke geometry around both carotid arteries.

Once on your back with hooks fully elevated, arch your hips upward and squeeze your elbows toward your sternum. Rotate your choking wrist slightly toward the ceiling to increase compression on the carotid arteries. Maintain constant hook elevation to prevent stacking. Apply pressure progressively and smoothly, and release immediately upon your opponent's tap signal.

common_counters.counter: Opponent postures up explosively and strips the choking grip with both hands before it locks
common_counters.your_response: Transition to butterfly sweep immediately as their posture recovery lifts their center of gravity and compromises their base, making them vulnerable to elevation

common_counters.counter: Opponent drives forward aggressively to stack and pass to side control, using pressure to nullify the choke angle
common_counters.your_response: Maintain the grip and guard your closed guard by locking your legs around their waist, then reattempt the choke from closed guard or transition to high elbow variation

common_counters.counter: Opponent circles toward the choking arm side to reduce the angle and create slack in the choke
common_counters.your_response: Follow their rotation with your hips and hooks, maintaining the choke angle by hip-escaping in the same direction they are circling to stay ahead of their movement

common_counters.counter: Opponent tucks chin deep and uses hand fighting to prevent wrist from contacting the carotid
common_counters.your_response: Switch to a high elbow Marcelotine configuration which bypasses chin defense by attacking over the jaw line, or transition to an arm-in variation trapping their fighting hand

common_errors.error: Attempting the guillotine without first breaking the opponent's posture and getting their head below shoulder level
common_errors.consequence: The opponent easily postures out of the loose grip and may pass your guard during the failed attempt while you are committed to the choke
common_errors.correction: Always snap the head down first and confirm the opponent's posture is broken before threading the choking arm; use collar ties and two-on-one grips to break posture

common_errors.error: Falling back before the grip is fully secured and locked with both hands
common_errors.consequence: The opponent strips the loose grip during the transition and ends up in top position with you flat on your back without guard hooks engaged
common_errors.correction: Complete the full grip lock sequence (thread arm, connect hands, pinch elbows) before initiating the fall-back; patience here prevents position loss

common_errors.error: Crossing ankles behind the opponent's back instead of maintaining independent butterfly hooks
common_errors.consequence: Loss of all elevation capability removes the stretching force needed to finish the choke and allows opponent to stack and pass freely
common_errors.correction: Keep hooks independent with feet under the opponent's inner thighs; use active hook elevation throughout the finish to maintain opposing forces

common_errors.error: Squeezing with the arms only instead of using full-body mechanics including hip arch and hook elevation
common_errors.consequence: Arm fatigue sets in quickly and the choke lacks sufficient pressure to compress the carotid arteries against a defending opponent
common_errors.correction: Engage your entire posterior chain by arching hips, driving hooks upward, and pulling elbows to sternum simultaneously for maximum compression

common_errors.error: Leaving space between your chest and the opponent's head and neck during the grip lock
common_errors.consequence: The gap allows the opponent to tuck their chin, insert a hand to fight the grip, or create enough slack to breathe and defend
common_errors.correction: Pull the opponent's head tight against your chest before and during the grip lock; eliminate all space by curling your upper body around their head

common_errors.error: Choking across the windpipe with a flat forearm instead of angling the wrist blade against the carotid
common_errors.consequence: Creates an air choke that is painful but slow, gives the opponent more time to escape, and increases risk of tracheal injury
common_errors.correction: Angle the radius bone of the choking wrist against the lateral neck to target the carotid artery for a cleaner blood choke with faster onset

training_progressions.focus: Choking arm placement and grip configuration
training_progressions.description: Practice threading the choking arm, positioning the wrist blade on the carotid, and locking different grip configurations (Gable, S-grip, palm-to-palm) against a stationary partner. Focus on eliminating space and achieving proper forearm angle on the neck.

training_progressions.focus: Snap-down entries and recognizing head-down opportunities
training_progressions.description: Drill snap-downs from butterfly guard against a partner who provides moderate forward pressure. Practice reading when the head drops below shoulder level and transitioning from the snap to the arm thread in one fluid motion.

training_progressions.focus: Fall-back, hook elevation, and full-body squeeze coordination
training_progressions.description: With the grip already secured, practice the fall-back and finish against a compliant partner. Focus on coordinating hook elevation with hip arch and elbow squeeze. Partner provides graduated resistance to the finish.

training_progressions.focus: Integrating guillotine threats with butterfly sweep attacks
training_progressions.description: Combine guillotine entries with butterfly sweeps against a live partner. When the partner defends the choke, attack the sweep; when they defend the sweep, attack the choke. Develop the ability to flow between both threats seamlessly.

training_progressions.focus: Full resistance positional sparring from butterfly guard
training_progressions.description: Positional sparring starting in butterfly guard bottom with all attacks available. Work on reading opponent reactions under full resistance and executing the guillotine when genuine openings appear rather than forcing the technique.

flashcards.question: What anatomical structures does the Guillotine Choke from Butterfly Guard primarily target?
flashcards.answer: The guillotine primarily targets the carotid arteries on both sides of the neck to create a blood choke. The choking wrist blade compresses the near-side carotid while the forearm and bicep compress the far-side carotid against the opponent's own shoulder. Secondary pressure may also affect the trachea if the forearm angle is not precise, which should be avoided in favor of clean arterial compression.

flashcards.question: How do you recognize when the choke has reached the point where escape becomes nearly impossible for the defender?
flashcards.answer: The point of no escape occurs when the grip is fully locked with elbows pinched, the opponent's head is pulled tight against your chest with no space, and your hooks are elevated with hips arched to create the stretching force. At this stage the opponent cannot posture, cannot strip the grip with hand fighting, and cannot stack because the hooks prevent forward drive. Their only remaining option is to tap.

flashcards.question: What grip and positional control must be established before committing to the fall-back finish?
flashcards.answer: Before falling back, you must have the choking arm fully threaded under the chin with wrist on the carotid, both hands locked together in a secure grip configuration, elbows pinched tight with no slack, the opponent's head pulled against your chest, and far-side control through an overhook or elbow clamp. Falling back without all of these in place risks losing the grip and ending up in a worse position.

flashcards.question: Your opponent starts to posture up while you have a loose guillotine grip - what adjustment prevents escape?
flashcards.answer: Rather than fighting the posture with arm strength alone, immediately transition to a butterfly sweep by driving your hook on the same side as your choking arm upward while pulling the opponent's upper body across with the guillotine grip. Their posture recovery raises their center of gravity and weakens their base, making the sweep high-percentage. If the sweep fails, you can re-engage the guillotine when they return to a defensive posture.

flashcards.question: What is the most common finishing error that allows opponents to survive the Guillotine from Butterfly Guard?
flashcards.answer: The most common error is squeezing only with the arms while neglecting full-body mechanics. Without hip arch and hook elevation, the choke lacks the opposing forces needed to compress the carotid arteries against a resisting opponent. The arms fatigue quickly and the opponent can outlast the squeeze. The correction is to engage the entire posterior chain: arch hips upward, drive hooks into the thighs, and pull elbows toward the sternum simultaneously.

flashcards.question: How should you adjust your grip if the opponent tucks their chin to block the choking arm from reaching the carotid?
flashcards.answer: Switch to a high elbow Marcelotine configuration by rotating the choking elbow above the opponent's spine and pulling the wrist deeper across the throat. This angle attacks over the jaw line and bypasses chin defense because the forearm compresses the neck from a higher angle that the tucked chin cannot block. Alternatively, transition to an arm-in guillotine that traps the opponent's defending hand alongside their neck.

flashcards.question: What are the critical safety considerations when applying the Guillotine Choke from Butterfly Guard in training?
flashcards.answer: Apply pressure slowly and progressively over 3-5 seconds minimum, never snapping or jerking the choke. Always ensure your partner has clear access to tap with at least one hand or can give a verbal tap. Release immediately upon any tap signal, vocal sound, or sign of distress. Never use neck cranking as a finishing mechanic. Avoid training this technique on partners with existing neck injuries, and always check on your partner after a deep choke attempt.

flashcards.question: How should you immediately release the Guillotine Choke after your training partner taps?
flashcards.answer: Immediately release all choking arm pressure by opening your grip and removing your arm from around the opponent's neck. Lower your hooks so they can move freely. If the partner appears dazed or was close to unconsciousness, help them to a seated position and monitor their breathing and consciousness. Do not celebrate or move away before confirming your partner is fully alert and responsive.

flashcards.question: What role do the butterfly hooks play in the finishing mechanics of this choke?
flashcards.answer: The butterfly hooks create the upward elevation force that stretches the opponent's torso away from their head while the choking grip pulls the head toward you. This opposing-force dynamic tightens the choke geometry around the neck without requiring excessive arm strength. Without active hook elevation, the opponent can compact their body, reduce pressure on the neck, and potentially stack forward to escape. The hooks are the primary differentiator between this variant and other guillotine finishes.

flashcards.question: In competition, how do you finish the Guillotine when an opponent attempts to stack and drive through your guard?
flashcards.answer: When the opponent drives forward to stack, close your guard around their waist to prevent them from passing to side control while maintaining the guillotine grip. From closed guard, you can still finish by arching your hips and squeezing. If the closed guard guillotine stalls, use the grip to threaten while working to re-establish butterfly hooks for the stronger finish, or transition to a high elbow variation that maintains pressure even when stacked.

defender.name: from Butterfly Guard Defender
defender.description: Defend the Guillotine Choke from Butterfly Guard. Recognition cues, posture recovery, grip stripping, and escape techniques to neutralize this choke safely.
defender.overview: Defending the Guillotine Choke from Butterfly Guard requires early recognition of the attack setup and immediate posture recovery before the grip locks. The defender faces a compound threat because the butterfly hooks create elevation that assists the choke finish while simultaneously threatening sweeps. The primary defensive priority is preventing the attacker from locking a tight grip configuration, because once a high-elbow or chin strap grip is fully secured with hooks engaged and the attacker falls back, escape becomes significantly more difficult. Understanding whether to posture up, drive forward, or circle to create slack determines survival in each phase of the attack.
key_principles: Protect the neck proactively by keeping chin tucked and posture upright to deny head-down entries before they happen
Address the grip immediately when you feel an arm threading under your chin, before the attacker can lock both hands
Drive forward into the attacker rather than pulling head straight backward, which extends the neck into the choke
Clear or neutralize the butterfly hooks to eliminate the elevation force that powers the finish
Circle toward the choking arm side to reduce the choking angle and create slack in the grip
Maintain composure and work methodically through escape sequences rather than panicking and burning energy
recognition_cues: Opponent snaps your head down with a collar tie or two-on-one grip while maintaining active butterfly hooks under your thighs
You feel an arm threading under your chin from the front while the opponent maintains a seated upright posture
Opponent's hips begin to withdraw and shift backward while their hooks maintain upward pressure on your thighs, indicating the fall-back finish is beginning
Grip tightening sensation around your neck combined with the opponent curling their upper body around your head and pulling elbows inward

defensive_options.action: Posture up and strip the grip by peeling the choking wrist away from your neck with both hands while driving your hips back
defensive_options.when_to_use: Early in the attack when the grip is not yet fully locked and you still have upright posture with base
defensive_options.if_successful: Return to neutral butterfly guard top position with posture restored and immediate passing opportunity
defensive_options.risk: If the grip is already deep, attempting to strip it while posturing may extend your neck into the choke

defensive_options.action: Drive forward aggressively to stack the attacker flat on their back, pinning their hips to the mat and eliminating hook elevation
defensive_options.when_to_use: When the attacker has already begun falling back and you cannot strip the grip cleanly from upright
defensive_options.if_successful: Attacker loses hook elevation and finishing leverage; you end up in their closed guard where the choke angle is weaker
defensive_options.risk: If you drive without clearing the hooks, the attacker can redirect your momentum into a sweep

defensive_options.action: Circle toward the choking arm side while keeping your head tight to the attacker's body to create slack in the choke
defensive_options.when_to_use: When the grip is locked but the attacker has not yet fully committed to the fall-back, giving you time to change angles
defensive_options.if_successful: The angle change creates enough slack to extract your head or transition to a Von Flue counter position
defensive_options.risk: Circling slowly or in the wrong direction can tighten the choke rather than loosen it

defensive_options.action: Clear one butterfly hook by pushing the knee to the mat and immediately driving through to pass to side control
defensive_options.when_to_use: When you recognize the guillotine threat early and can address the hooks before the choke locks
defensive_options.if_successful: Eliminating the hook removes the elevation force needed for the finish and gives you a clear passing lane
defensive_options.risk: Reaching down to clear hooks while your posture is broken can deepen the guillotine grip

escape_paths: Posture up explosively and strip the choking wrist with two-on-one grip fighting before the lock is secured
Drive forward to stack the attacker flat, eliminating hook elevation and passing to side control or closed guard top
Circle toward the choking arm side to reduce the angle and create slack for head extraction

favorable_outcomes.how: Drive through the guillotine attempt and stack the attacker flat, clearing the hooks and landing in their closed guard on top where the choke angle is significantly weakened and you can work to strip the grip
Strip the grip early before it locks by peeling the choking wrist and recovering posture, returning to a neutral butterfly guard top position with passing opportunities

common_errors.error: Pulling the head straight backward to escape the choke
common_errors.consequence: Extends the neck directly into the choking pressure, tightening the grip and accelerating blood flow restriction to the brain
common_errors.correction: Drive forward into the attacker or circle laterally toward the choking arm side; never pull the head away from the body applying the choke

common_errors.error: Ignoring a loose early grip and continuing to pass as if the threat is not present
common_errors.consequence: The attacker locks the grip while you are focused on passing, and by the time you address the choke it is fully secured and much harder to escape
common_errors.correction: Address any hand around your neck immediately when it is loose and easy to strip; a two-second delay can be the difference between easy escape and survival mode

common_errors.error: Driving forward without clearing the butterfly hooks first
common_errors.consequence: The attacker redirects your forward momentum into a butterfly sweep, landing you on your back with the guillotine still locked
common_errors.correction: Clear at least one hook or pin the opponent's hips before driving forward, eliminating the elevation capability that enables both the sweep and the choke finish

common_errors.error: Panicking and using explosive energy without a technical escape plan
common_errors.consequence: Rapid energy depletion with no positional improvement, leaving you exhausted and still in the choke with less ability to defend
common_errors.correction: Stay calm, tuck the chin, and systematically work through escape options: strip grip first, then drive or circle, addressing one problem at a time

flashcards.question: How do you recognize that a Guillotine Choke from Butterfly Guard is being set up?
flashcards.answer: Key recognition cues include the opponent snapping your head down with a collar tie while maintaining butterfly hooks, feeling an arm threading under your chin from the front, and the opponent shifting to a more upright seated posture while gripping your neck. Early recognition before the grip locks is critical because escape difficulty increases dramatically once both hands are connected.

flashcards.question: What is the safest way to signal a tap when caught in a Guillotine from Butterfly Guard?
flashcards.answer: Tap clearly and repeatedly on the opponent's body, your own body, or the mat with your hand. If your hands are trapped, use a verbal tap by saying 'tap' clearly or making any vocal sound. You can also tap with your feet on the mat. Tap early before losing consciousness. There is no advantage to fighting a fully locked guillotine past the point of safety in training.

flashcards.question: What is the primary defensive priority when you feel a guillotine grip being established from butterfly guard?
flashcards.answer: The primary priority is preventing the grip from locking. Strip the choking wrist with both hands immediately while it is still loose, before the attacker can connect their hands. A loose single-hand guillotine grip is relatively easy to peel away, but once both hands lock together with elbows pinched, the grip becomes extremely difficult to break and your options narrow to angle changes and stacking rather than grip stripping.

flashcards.question: Why is pulling your head straight backward the wrong escape strategy against a butterfly guillotine?
flashcards.answer: Pulling the head backward extends the neck directly into the choking forearm, tightening the compression on the carotid arteries. It also increases the distance between your torso and the attacker's body, which is exactly the stretching force the attacker wants. The correct approach is to drive forward to compress the space and eliminate the choking angle, or circle laterally toward the choking arm to create slack.

flashcards.question: What defensive options remain if the attacker has already locked a full grip and begun falling back with hook elevation?
flashcards.answer: At this late stage, your best option is to drive forward aggressively to stack the attacker, pinning their hips to the mat to eliminate hook elevation power. Simultaneously work to clear at least one hook by pushing the knee to the mat. If you can flatten them and remove the hooks, the choke loses most of its finishing power and you can work to strip the grip from top position. If you cannot escape, tap immediately rather than risking unconsciousness.

training_progressions.focus: Identifying guillotine setups and maintaining defensive posture
training_progressions.description: Practice recognizing the snap-down and arm-thread entries while maintaining chin-tucked upright posture. Partner initiates guillotine entries at slow speed while you focus on keeping your head above shoulder level and reacting immediately to any hand around the neck.

training_progressions.focus: Removing the choking grip before it locks
training_progressions.description: Partner secures a loose guillotine grip and you practice two-on-one grip stripping while recovering posture. Graduate to scenarios where the grip is progressively tighter, learning the feel of when stripping is viable versus when you need to switch to driving or circling.

training_progressions.focus: Escaping locked guillotines through forward pressure
training_progressions.description: Partner locks a full guillotine grip from butterfly guard and falls back. Practice driving forward to stack, clearing hooks, and landing in top position. Work on maintaining calm under the choke pressure while executing the technical escape sequence methodically.

training_progressions.focus: Full resistance defense from butterfly guard top
training_progressions.description: Positional sparring where partner starts in butterfly guard with guillotine as a primary weapon. Defend the guillotine under full resistance while also working to pass the guard. Develops realistic timing for when to strip grips, when to drive, and when to tap.
